*Critical data revealing why managed infrastructure and secure coding practices matter more than ever in the age of AI-assisted development*


The rise of AI-powered app building has created an unprecedented security paradox. While[85%](https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2025/10/state-of-developer-ecosystem-2025/) of developers regularly used AI coding tools in JetBrains' 2025 survey, research shows that[45%](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) of AI-generated samples failed security tests in Veracode's controlled evaluation. For non-technical founders and builders using conversational AI to create apps, this gap between rapid development speed and security risk creates real concern.


Floot addresses this challenge through an MCP connector that works with supported AI assistants and[managed app infrastructure](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) , including built-in authentication, a Postgres database, and backend hosting, while builders remain responsible for their application's security.


## **Key Takeaways**


- **AI code introduces measurable risk:**[45% of AI-generated](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) samples failed security tests in Veracode's controlled evaluation, making security reviews essential.
- **Security findings surge in enterprise repositories:** Monthly findings in Apiiro's analysis increased[10× over six](https://apiiro.com/blog/4x-velocity-10x-vulnerabilities-ai-coding-assistants-are-shipping-more-risks/) months, exceeding 10,000 in June 2025.
- **Language choice correlates with vulnerability patterns:** TypeScript showed[2.50%-7.14%](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) in one examined sample, but language choice alone does not guarantee security.
- **Governance gaps create exposure:**[81% of surveyed security](https://cycode.com/press/report-shadow-ai-crisis-looms-as-100-of-companies-have-ai-generated-code-but-81-of-security-teams-lack-visibility/) teams lacked full visibility into AI use, highlighting oversight needs.
- **Managed infrastructure reduces setup risks:** Floot provides[built-in sign-in](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) ,[managed Postgres](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) , and hosting while builders remain responsible for app-level security.


## **Understanding the Landscape of AI Code Generation and Security Risks**


The rapid adoption of AI coding tools has fundamentally changed how applications are built. Understanding the baseline risk profile of AI-generated code helps builders make informed decisions about which platforms and practices protect their applications.


### **1. 45% of AI-generated samples failed security tests in Veracode's controlled evaluation**


Nearly half of AI-generated code samples,[45%, failed security validation](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) in Veracode's controlled evaluation against OWASP Top 10 vulnerability classes. This failure rate highlights why relying solely on AI output without application security reviews creates significant exposure. The controlled test environment focused on security-sensitive coding tasks, revealing patterns where AI tools struggle with proper security implementation.


### **2. 62% of AI-generated solutions contain design flaws or known vulnerabilities**


Cloud Security Alliance research found that[62% of generated solutions](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-codegen-vulnerability-debt-20260406-csa/) contain design flaws or known security vulnerabilities. These issues range from improper input validation to insecure data handling patterns. The findings emphasize that while AI accelerates development, it does not automatically incorporate security best practices, making independent testing important for builders without security expertise.


### **3. 87.9% of analyzed files had no detectable CWE-mapped vulnerabilities**


On a more nuanced note, academic analysis found that[87.9% of sampled files](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) did not contain identifiable vulnerabilities mapped to Common Weakness Enumeration categories. This suggests that most files in the analyzed sample had no detectable CWE-mapped vulnerabilities, although static analysis cannot establish that the code is free of security risks. Proper security practices and platform protections remain essential.


### **4. AI-related CVEs increased 34.6% year-over-year in 2025**


The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures related to AI systems reached 2,130 in 2025, a[34.6% increase](https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/threat-landscape/fault-lines-in-the-ai-ecosystem-trendai-state-of-ai-security-report) from the previous year. This historical figure does not establish that the same growth rate continued in 2026 or 2027. The expanding vulnerability database underscores the importance of choosing platforms that maintain security updates and protections as new threats emerge.


### **5. Monthly security findings surged 10× in Apiiro's enterprise repository analysis**


Apiiro's deep code analysis revealed that repositories analyzed at Fortune 50 enterprises saw monthly security findings rise[10× to over 10,000](https://apiiro.com/blog/4x-velocity-10x-vulnerabilities-ai-coding-assistants-are-shipping-more-risks/) in just six months between December 2024 and June 2025. This surge occurred alongside increased AI-assisted code volume, demonstrating how velocity gains can amplify the burden of security review without proper safeguards.


## **AI-Generated App Security Statistics on Vulnerability Growth**


The acceleration of AI-generated vulnerabilities represents one of the most significant shifts in application security. These statistics reveal the scale and speed of emerging risks.


### **6. 74 AI-linked CVEs tracked by Vibe Security Radar through March 2026**


Georgia Tech's Vibe Security Radar confirmed[74 AI-linked](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-codegen-vulnerability-debt-20260406-csa/) CVEs through March 2026 in the Cloud Security Alliance's published research summary. The findings highlight the need for ongoing security review as AI-generated code becomes more widely used. This documented set of vulnerability cases does not establish the total number of defects across all AI-assisted applications.


### **7. Privilege-escalation paths rose 322% in Apiiro's enterprise analysis**


In Apiiro's enterprise analysis, privilege-escalation paths increased by[322% in AI-assisted code](https://apiiro.com/blog/4x-velocity-10x-vulnerabilities-ai-coding-assistants-are-shipping-more-risks/) compared with the study's baseline. These vulnerabilities can allow attackers to gain unauthorized access to protected resources and data, making them particularly dangerous in production applications. The increase shows why builders need to test authorization decisions rather than assuming generated code implements proper access controls.


### **8. 97% of surveyed organizations reported GenAI-related security incidents**


Capgemini Research Institute found that[97% of organizations](https://www.capgemini.com/insights/research-library/generative-ai-in-cybersecurity/) surveyed reported security incidents related to generative AI usage in the preceding year. This near-universal reported impact underscores the importance of security controls. The statistic covers broader GenAI incidents, including prompt injection, shadow AI, and misuse; it is not a measurement of confirmed breaches caused specifically by AI-generated application code.


### **9. AI-assisted developers produced 3–4× more commits in Apiiro's enterprise analysis**


In Apiiro's enterprise analysis, developers using AI tools produced[3 – 4× more commits](https://apiiro.com/blog/4x-velocity-10x-vulnerabilities-ai-coding-assistants-are-shipping-more-risks/) than their non-AI-assisted peers. While this velocity can create an advantage, larger combined changes can also make reviewing authorization and data flows harder. The acceleration demands security measures that can keep pace with development speed, making application-level reviews and automated checks increasingly important.


### **10. 25% of Y Combinator startups had 95%+ AI-generated codebases in Winter 2025**


Y Combinator reported that[25% of its Winter](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-codegen-vulnerability-debt-20260406-csa/) 2025 batch had codebases with 95% of lines generated by language models. This trend toward heavily AI-generated applications makes security testing important. The statistic refers to that specific historical startup cohort and does not show that all startups or all published apps rely on AI to the same extent.


### **11. 85% of developers regularly used AI coding tools in JetBrains' 2025 survey**


The JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey found that[85% of developers](https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2025/10/state-of-developer-ecosystem-2025/) regularly used AI tools for coding and development in 2025. This mainstream adoption means security considerations for AI-generated code affect many development teams. The widespread integration of AI into development workflows makes understanding AI-related security risks essential for builders at all levels.


## **Common CVE Vulnerabilities in AI-Assisted Applications**


Certain vulnerability types appear consistently in AI-generated code. Understanding these patterns helps builders choose platforms that address these specific weaknesses through built-in protections.


### **12. 86% of AI-generated samples failed XSS defenses in focused tests**


Cross-site scripting remains a persistent weakness, with[86% of relevant samples](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) in XSS-focused security tests failing to implement proper defenses. This vulnerability allows attackers to inject malicious scripts into web applications. The high failure rate in controlled tests demonstrates difficulty with script-injection defenses, while application-level output encoding and security reviews remain essential.


### **13. 12% mean security pass rate on log-injection tasks in 2026**


In Veracode's 2026 log-injection test cases, AI models achieved a mean security[pass rate of approximately 12%](https://view.ceros.com/veracode/genai-code-security-report2026) , showing substantial difficulty with CWE-117 protections. This weakness occurs when generated code fails to handle untrusted input before writing to logs, potentially allowing attackers to manipulate log records. The benchmark reflects controlled coding tasks, not the percentage of deployed applications with log-injection vulnerabilities.


### **14. 72% of Java AI-generated code failed security tests in 2025**


Java showed particularly concerning results in Veracode's 2025 evaluation, with a[72% security failure rate](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) across the tested coding tasks. This language-specific benchmark highlights the need for careful security review. The result concerns controlled tasks rather than deployed Java applications and does not establish that choosing a different language alone will prevent vulnerabilities in AI-generated code.


### **15. 19.6% average package-hallucination rate across tested coding models**


USENIX Security researchers found an average[19.6% package hallucination](https://www.usenix.org/publications/loginonline/we-have-package-you-comprehensive-analysis-package-hallucinations-code) rate across 16 tested coding models. These hallucinated recommendations refer to package names that do not exist in the relevant repositories. Such recommendations can create opportunities for supply-chain attacks if malicious actors register the invented names. The figure is an average across the tested models, not a universal failure rate for every AI-generated application.


### **16. SQL injection vulnerabilities average 8.76 CVSS score in analyzed AI code**


Among the severe weaknesses in the analyzed AI-generated code, SQL injection carried an average[CVSS score of 8.76](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) . Managed database access combined with correctly implemented parameterized queries can help prevent injection vulnerabilities. This is why[managed Postgres databases](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) should be paired with application-specific permissions and secure queries. Database hosting alone does not automatically prevent SQL injection.


## **Implementing Secure Coding Practices with AI Coding Tools**


Security-conscious builders can significantly reduce risk through informed platform choices and development practices. These statistics reveal where attention matters most.


### **17. TypeScript showed lowest vulnerability prevalence in the examined study**


Academic analysis found that TypeScript exhibited[2.50%-7.14%](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) prevalence of identified vulnerabilities among the examined language-and-tool groups. This observational result does not prove TypeScript alone makes generated applications secure. Floot projects use TypeScript and React by default. When you[build through AI assistants](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/build-from-claude-and-chatgpt) , static type checking helps catch certain errors while security testing and review remain necessary.


### **18. Python showed higher vulnerability rates in the examined study**


In contrast, Python code attributed to AI tools showed[16.18%-18.50%](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) vulnerability prevalence in the analyzed dataset. These higher observed rates compared with TypeScript suggest that language choice may correlate with vulnerability patterns in the sampled files. The results do not establish a universal ranking of languages or prove that Python itself causes the observed security issues.


### **19. JavaScript showed 8.66%-8.99% vulnerability rates in the analyzed study**


JavaScript falls in the middle range with[8.66%-8.99%](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) vulnerability prevalence in the examined AI-generated samples. While lower than Python in the study, these rates were higher than TypeScript's observed prevalence. The difference reflects the particular files, tools, and analysis method involved; it should not be treated as proof that JavaScript is inherently less secure than TypeScript.


### **20. 75.8% of surveyed respondents believed AI generates more secure code**


Despite empirical evidence of AI-generated vulnerabilities,[75.8% of respondents](https://snyk.io/blog/securing-genai-development-with-snyk/) in Snyk's survey believed AI code was more secure than human-written code. This perception gap creates risk when developers skip security reviews of AI output. The disconnect between confidence and measured security outcomes highlights the need for independent testing rather than relying on generated code or managed infrastructure alone.


## **Leveraging Application Security Tools for AI-Generated Code**


Traditional security tools can identify vulnerabilities in AI-generated applications. Managed infrastructure reduces certain configuration risks but does not replace application scanning or code review.


### **21. 2,038 critical vulnerabilities found across scanned vibe-coded applications**


Escape.tech identified[2,038 highly critical vulnerabilities](https://escape.tech/state-of-security-of-vibe-coded-apps) across approximately 1,400 affected vibe-coded applications. These findings illustrate substantial security exposure in the scanned sample. The analysis demonstrates that AI-assisted applications can contain serious flaws that automated security assessments can detect, although the sample does not establish the prevalence of critical vulnerabilities across every app built with AI.


### **22. Over 400 leaked secrets discovered in vibe-coded applications**


Security researchers found[400+ leaked secrets](https://escape.tech/state-of-security-of-vibe-coded-apps) , including credentials and API keys, exposed in the studied vibe-coded applications. Proper secret management at the platform level can reduce the risk of credential exposure, although application code and integrations still require review. The prevalence of exposed credentials demonstrates a common failure pattern in applications built and deployed rapidly.


### **23. 175 instances of exposed PII found in vibe-coded apps**


Personally identifiable information, including financial details, appeared in[175 documented instances](https://escape.tech/state-of-security-of-vibe-coded-apps) across the vibe-coded applications studied by Escape.tech. Such exposure may create privacy and legal risks for application owners. The discovery of PII in published applications highlights how AI-generated software can inadvertently reveal sensitive data without proper security review and data handling practices.


### **24. 4%–20% of MCP repositories contained exploitable vulnerabilities**


Trend Micro's analysis of 19,000 open-source MCP repositories found that[4% to 20%](https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/threat-landscape/fault-lines-in-the-ai-ecosystem-trendai-state-of-ai-security-report) contained exploitable vulnerabilities. Understanding[how MCP works](https://floot.com/blog/what-is-mcp-a-simple-guide-to-model-context-protocol-for-ai-apps) helps builders evaluate which integrations and connections to trust. The cited research reports a range, but does not establish that the lower and upper values represent particular severity categories.


## **The Role of Static Code Analysis in AI-Assisted Development**


Static analysis tools provide automated vulnerability detection, but their effectiveness varies based on the AI tools and languages involved.


### **25. 42.6% of classified MCP vulnerabilities showed AI-generated code patterns**


Among classified vulnerabilities in MCP repositories,[42.6% exhibited signs](https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/threat-landscape/fault-lines-in-the-ai-ecosystem-trendai-state-of-ai-security-report) of AI-generated code according to Trend Micro's analysis. This correlation suggests AI-generated components deserve particular scrutiny in security reviews. However, identifying an AI-generated pattern does not by itself establish that AI was the cause of every vulnerability or that all AI-assisted MCP projects are insecure.


### **26. 63% of respondents reported suspected AI-involved attacks in 12 months**


Bitdefender's assessment found that[63% of respondents](https://businessinsights.bitdefender.com/research-ai-cyberattacks-target-majority-organizations) believed their organization experienced an attack involving AI within the preceding 12 months. Attackers are adopting AI capabilities alongside developers. The finding describes survey respondents' assessment of attacks rather than independent forensic confirmation, highlighting the need for security strategies that address both AI-assisted development and AI-enabled threats.


### **27. AI-enabled malicious breaches averaged $6 million in IBM's 2026 research**


IBM's 2026 breach-cost research found that AI-enabled malicious attacks had average breach[costs of $6 million](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-07-29-ibm-study-one-in-four-malicious-breaches-are-ai-enabled,-costing-companies-6-million-on-average) . This figure reflects incidents where attackers used AI, not specifically breaches of AI-generated applications. The financial impact reinforces the importance of prevention and response planning, without establishing a specific return on investment for any particular application-building platform.


## **Best Practices for Securing Your AI-Generated Apps**


Builders can substantially reduce their risk profile by choosing platforms with built-in security controls and following established practices for AI-assisted development.


### **28. Organizations extensively using security AI and automation saved $1.93M per breach**


IBM's 2026 research found that organizations extensively using AI and automation in security saved[$1.93M per breach](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach) compared with organizations using none. These findings concern dedicated security AI and automation rather than the security benefits of any particular app-building platform. The observed cost difference demonstrates the potential value of security measures in reducing breach impact and recovery costs.


### **29. Extensive security AI use was linked to an 80-day shorter breach lifecycle**


IBM's 2025 breach research found that organizations extensively using AI and automation in security reduced their breach lifecycle by[an average of 80 days](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2025-07-30-ibm-report-13-of-organizations-reported-breaches-of-ai-models-or-applications,-97-of-which-reported-lacking-proper-ai-access-controls) compared with those using none. The measurement combines identification and containment time; it is not a detection-only figure. The association highlights the potential value of automated monitoring and response without proving causation.


### **30. 81% of surveyed security teams lacked full visibility into AI usage**


Perhaps most concerning,[81% of surveyed security](https://cycode.com/press/report-shadow-ai-crisis-looms-as-100-of-companies-have-ai-generated-code-but-81-of-security-teams-lack-visibility/) teams lacked full visibility into how AI was used in their software development processes. This shadow AI problem can compound security risks by leaving activity outside established oversight. The governance gap highlights why documented AI usage and access permissions matter for organizational security, alongside the technical safeguards of any platform.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **How does AI code generation introduce new security risks?**


AI coding tools generate code based on patterns learned from training data, which may include insecure practices. Research shows that[45% of AI-generated](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) samples failed security tests in Veracode's controlled evaluation, while package-hallucination research reported an average[19.6% rate](https://www.usenix.org/publications/loginonline/we-have-package-you-comprehensive-analysis-package-hallucinations-code) across tested models. These risks increase when builders accept output without checking app logic, dependencies, and access controls.


### **Can static analysis tools effectively find vulnerabilities in AI-generated code?**


Static analysis tools can identify common vulnerability patterns in AI-generated code. In Trend Micro's MCP research,[42.6% of classified](https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/security/news/threat-landscape/fault-lines-in-the-ai-ecosystem-trendai-state-of-ai-security-report) vulnerabilities showed AI-generated code patterns, although this does not establish causation. For non-technical builders,[managed app infrastructure](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) can reduce setup risks while application scanning and security reviews remain important.


### **What are the most common types of vulnerabilities found in AI-assisted applications?**


Relevant controlled tests found[86% XSS failures](https://www.veracode.com/blog/genai-code-security-report/) and approximately a[12% log-injection pass rate](https://view.ceros.com/veracode/genai-code-security-report2026) . An academic analysis assigned SQL injection an[8.76 average](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.26103v1) CVSS score; Apiiro also found[322%](https://apiiro.com/blog/4x-velocity-10x-vulnerabilities-ai-coding-assistants-are-shipping-more-risks/) higher privilege-escalation paths in its enterprise comparison. These are different metrics from different samples, not a universal prevalence ranking.


### **How can non-technical builders ensure the security of apps they create with AI?**


Non-technical builders should prioritize secure database queries, input validation, appropriate user permissions, and independent testing. With[81% of surveyed security](https://cycode.com/press/report-shadow-ai-crisis-looms-as-100-of-companies-have-ai-generated-code-but-81-of-security-teams-lack-visibility/) teams lacking full AI-use visibility, clear permissions matter too. Floot provides[built-in authentication](https://floot.com/docs/integrations/whats-built-in) and hosting, but builders must review the generated app's access rules and behavior.


### **What role does continuous monitoring play in AI-generated app security?**


Logging and monitoring can improve visibility into application behavior, but effective breach detection may still require dedicated security tools and ongoing review. IBM's 2025 research reported a breach lifecycle shorter by[80 days among organizations](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2025-07-30-ibm-report-13-of-organizations-reported-breaches-of-ai-models-or-applications,-97-of-which-reported-lacking-proper-ai-access-controls) extensively using security AI and automation. That is a combined identification-and-containment comparison, not an AI-app-specific detection result.
